title: What the Caller Keeps
passages:
Mara's hand came off Nia's wrist finger by finger, unhurried, the way you set down a tool you're finished with, and then she crossed the ward and sat at the crank and started turning.

"Sorry," she said, to nobody.

"She does that," Nia said. She was rubbing her wrist. "Every few minutes. Like the handle's got her name on it."

The crank ran a dynamo the size of a bucket, and the dynamo charged the lamp cells along the wall — flat trays of gel that hold a charge the way a bad battery holds one, badly, and only if you keep working. Past them the cold-case rack ticked. One drawer still had its temperature strip in the green: the last of what Teo took.

Everything said in this air went into the Caller, so Wren kept her questions short and full of numbers.

"How many turns yesterday?"

The hammer came off its rest, tapped, and Mara's voice came out of the brass, clear as a woman at the next table. *Four hundred and six. Then I rested my arm.*

Nia made a sound like she'd been hit.

"Fine. That's fluent." Wren wet her mouth. "Your children's names."

The hammer tapped. Air moved in the throat of the bell, the beginning shape of a word, and then nothing but the click of the mechanism resetting itself.

"Ask if she sang," Salas said from the edge of the light. His coat was still wet to the chest.

"Singing's air," Nia said. "Two syllables is air. She spent hers on him." She jerked her chin at Salas without looking at him. "Names go first. Always names."

"Fragments don't buy," Wren said. "I want that on the record before anyone gets generous. It only trades whole — one voice, left in its throat, with a hand flat on the brass while it goes in. And the leaving takes the memory of the giving. You keep the hole. You don't keep the reason."

"I don't remember deciding," Mara said pleasantly, cranking.

Dey had drifted half a step toward the bell. Wren put her arm out and he stopped against it.

"You've got the only scrubber that fits Teo," she said, "so shut up."

She set Salas's slate on the cold-case lid to free both hands — the drawer with the green strip, cold enough to ache through her palm — and thumbed the wheel back through fourteen months of a man cracking an air valve to a woman he couldn't name, looking for the mark she wanted. It took a while. Nia watched her do it and didn't say anything, which was worse than being called a coward.

When Wren picked the slate up the cell read zero.

She turned it over. Turned it back. Cold does that to a cell; below the Line the cold gets into everything and stays. Four plays left in the log, and the log lived in the cell, and the cell was gone.

"That was the hair," Nia said. Her voice was very level. "I hadn't got to the hair."

"I know."

"Say the rest of it."

"The rest of it is I put it on the cold," Wren said. "I did that."

Nia looked at the dead slate a moment longer, then went and stood by her mother's crank, where the light was.

Wren thumbed her own slate awake instead. Fifty-two minutes sat in it, her gap, the thing she'd never explained to anybody on the Marrow, and inside the gap a mark in her own handwriting she had never played for a living soul.

The timer's hammer lifted toward its rest.

She put her thumb on the mark and the speaker leaked half a second before she clamped it into her palm: her own voice, thin, breathing on a scrubber, counting something down, and then, flat and close, *—up, all of it, up—*, and cut.

Salas got to the bell before Wren had her slate back in her pocket.

He didn't hurry. He came across the ward with his hand out flat, palm down, the way you walk up to a dog somebody told you was friendly.

"Take mine," he said.

The hammer lifted off its rest and hung there, waiting on the room. The crank kept its rhythm behind him. Mara said, "Mind the governor," to nobody in particular.

"Mara," Salas said, to the brass. "That's the word. Fourteen months I've had it in my mouth and no use for it. Cut it out of me and hand it back to her with the rest of her."

Wren caught his wrist. Cold as the drawer, and the old rope scars standing up on it in ridges.

"Flat palm on the brass while it goes in," she said. "You're a hand's width short, and I'd like you to stay short."

"Then take your arm off me."

"You heard yourself for fourteen months. I heard you too — topside, on the wire, and in here a minute ago." She kept hold. "Valve and rattle. Half a word, then the crack. That's not a voice, that's what's left after a voice has been spent down to thread on an air valve. Fragments. Same as hers. Fluent on turns, dead on names."

"Play it back to me, then."

"The log's dead. I put it on the cold." She let that sit for exactly as long as it needed to. "You watched me do it."

"I watched you drop a man's fourteen months in the drink because your hands were cold," Salas said. "There's a coat on my back somebody gave me at the low gate and a berth with a number on it, and I never earned either. One word out of ten thousand isn't going to be missed."

"You'll surface with the coat and the number and nothing left to say at a window." Wren nodded at the brass. "That's the trade. It doesn't take the word out of your mouth. It takes the mouth. You keep the hole, you don't keep the reason, and whatever you were going to say to her when she's up on the high ground with her kids — you won't have it. You'll stand there pleasant as a turn count."

"He's got a coat," Nia said from the crank. "I've got a mother."

Behind Wren the slate in her pocket was still warm from her own hand, and the Caller had half a second of her in it now — her breath on a scrubber, *up, all of it, up.* It didn't buy anything. It didn't need to. The thing kept whatever fell into the air whether it was worth keeping or not, and it kept it in her voice, and somewhere under this ward there were fifty-two minutes of her that had already gone the same way and never come back with a reason attached.

Salas took his hand out of the light. He looked at the empty cradle on the rack, then at Nia, then at the bell, and something in his face closed like a hatch.

"Fourteen months," he said. "Fourteen months I'm the only man in this room with a name in his mouth. Hers is gone, the girl's got a mother-shaped hole, and you — you had a mark in your hand a minute ago and you nearly spent it by accident in front of the whole ward." He wiped his mouth with the back of his wrist. "And now you're stood there telling me the one thing I've got left is counterfeit."

Dey came off the seaward wall and put his shoulder between Wren and the light.

"Then take mine," he said. "I'm the one with hours in me. Take a fistful, give her the kids' names, and we all go up and be sick over the side."

"Back up."

"I've got a whole voice." His hand was already coming up, flat, palm down, copying Salas without knowing he was doing it.

Wren got two fingers in his collar and set him back half a step. "Flat palm on the brass is the door. You're a hand's width off it and that's where you're staying."

"You put yours on in about a minute."

"Maybe I do." She kept the collar. "Hold still. I want you to hear this standing up, not sat down."

Dey's slate rode inside his suit on a wire to the collar, the way they all did, and it was warm, because he was warm, which was more than the rest of the room could say. She thumbed the wheel back to the place she'd found on the wire two nights ago with Salas breathing on her neck, and turned the gain up so the ward got it too.

His own voice came out of the little speaker, thin and pleased with itself. *All clear up here.*

Under it the level line ran flat, which is the sound of nothing arriving. Four seconds of flat. Then him again, the same three words, the same cheerful lift on *here*, a man reading his own card because he'd forgot he'd already read it.

She let it run out and stopped the wheel with her thumb.

"Again," Dey said.

"That's the lot. Twice in nine seconds, four seconds between them, and a hole in the middle you can't account for."

"Set's cold. Cell's low. You said so about Salas's."

"My slate doesn't care about cold." She held it up so he could watch the timestamp crawl. "It writes down what the mic hears. That's all a slate is. And what it heard was you telling the wire you were fine, and then you telling the wire you were fine."

The crank kept its rhythm behind him. Overhead the hammer hung off its rest, waiting on the room to say something worth keeping.

"Say the rest," Dey said.

"The rest is Sol heard it. Salas heard it. Neither of them told you, because you'd have gone down another ten meters to prove the gap wasn't there." She let go of his collar. "That's what a hero sounds like from topside. Same three words twice, in a voice with holes in it."

He didn't step back. He was fair about it, which she hadn't expected, and level, which was worse.

"You're a coward," he said.

"I've been called worse by better wet."

"You've got a mark in your hand you've never played for anyone and fifty-two minutes you won't explain, and you're stood there pricing everybody else's hours off a dead log." He nodded at the brass. "And I've got spares. Years in the tank, and nobody's taken one off me yet. You've got one voice and you already spent part of it somewhere and came back not knowing what for."

"That's the shape of it," Wren said.

"Then stop counting my money and spend yours."

Salas laughed once, without any pleasure in it, and turned his back on the three of them, which from Salas was practically an apology.

Nia hadn't moved from the dynamo. She had the crank handle in her fist, still swinging a little off the last of its travel, close enough to her mother that she could have touched her without leaning. She was watching Wren with her chin up, the way she'd watched her drop the slate on the cold.

Mara looked up from the bucket-sized dynamo at nothing in particular. "That's better," she said, agreeable as weather. Then she reached out and closed her hand around her daughter's wrist, the way she had an hour ago, finger by finger, unhurried, and did not let go.

Overhead the timer's hammer lifted the rest of the way and stayed there.

Wren crossed the ward with the slate in her fist and the cold of the drawer still in that hand. Three steps, and Nia didn't shift, so she went around the crank instead of through it, into the bad light between the bell's frame and the wall.

The Caller hung at chest height, green at the seams, its throat open, the hammer cocked above it on a clockwork arm. Beside it the governor spun — two brass flyweights on a spindle, and the whole trick of a governor is that when the load comes on, the weights fly out and slow the thing down so it doesn't run away from you. Its hum had a wobble in it. Everything in the room had a wobble in it.

She turned her slate over and looked at the mark before she touched it. Eleven seconds on the counter. The trace ran unbroken end to end, no flatline in the middle, nothing stepped out and nothing repeated. Whole. Whatever else she'd been, eleven months ago, she'd been careful.

"You said fragments don't buy," Dey said behind her.

"They don't."

"So what's this?"

"This is me paying retail." She put her palm flat on the brass.

Then she pressed the slate's speaker grille against the open throat, hard enough to feel the metal give, and started the mark, so that her voice went into the bell through the brass instead of across the air. The ward heard nothing. She heard it in her wrist and her back teeth.

Her own voice, thinner than she remembered, counting down from five the flat way you count when your hands are full. A breath dragged through a scrubber, the wet catch in it. Then close, unhurried, like a woman telling somebody where to put their feet: *—up, all of it, up—*. Then the click of the record ending.

The governor's wobble went out of its hum. The flyweights came level, the note dropped, and along the wall the needle on the lamp cell lifted off its floor pin and stood up in the working range, and every tray of gel on the shelf took the charge and held it, and one of them came up bright enough to read by.

Mara's fingers came open off her daughter's wrist. Not all at once. Finger by finger, the same as before, unhurried, and then her hands went back to the crank and she started turning again, and she said, "There. That's better," to nobody at all.

Nia pulled her arm in and held it against her chest and didn't look at anybody.

Wren took her palm off the brass. The eleven seconds were gone out of her hand and into the throat of the thing, and she reached for the reason she'd kept them, the way you reach for a light switch in a house you've lived in for years.

There was no reason. There was a shape where a reason had been.

She still had the fact of it, laid out plain: she'd had eleven seconds in her own voice, she'd carried them eleven months, she had never once played them for a living soul. What she did not have was who they were for, or what she'd been saving them to say, or why it had mattered more than the fifty-two minutes around them. That was gone, and it had gone in the same motion as the giving, exactly the way she'd told the room it would.

"Itemize it," Salas said.

"I can't. That's the item."

She thumbed her slate awake — hers, alive, the little wedge of amber still lit in the corner, the light that comes on when the log and the body stop agreeing — and put it in her own hand rather than her own voice, because words are cheaper and they keep.

*Played my eleven seconds into the Caller at slack. In my own voice. On purpose, with my hand on the brass. Kept them eleven months for somebody. The somebody is gone. Not the cold, not the Line, not an accident.*

"What did it cost you?" Nia said. She had her mother's crank handle in her fist, swinging a little off the travel.

"Eleven seconds and the name of who they were for."

"That's all?"

"That's the whole invoice." Wren put the slate away. "You get the hole. You don't get the reason. It's tidy that way."

Dey said something about that which was mostly swear, and the air took it, and none of them had anything to add.

Above her the hammer came off its rest with a small dry sound, like a coin set down on a table.

The hammer came down and the Caller gave back a woman with all of her hours in her.

Wren had spent an hour listening to the woman at the crank, and that had been like listening to a parts list read out in a pleasant voice. Correct, on time, nothing behind it. This was not that. This was somebody talking to her kids from the next room with her hands full.

*Nia.*

The name went the length of the ward. Nia didn't move. She had the crank handle down by her thigh in her fist and she stood the way you stand on a deck when a big one is coming and you've already decided not to grab anything.

*Teo. He's in the second drawer with the green strip and he's cold enough. I stayed to keep you cold till somebody came. Keep the lid shut. Keep it shut after, if nobody comes.*

Unhurried, all of it, a woman telling somebody where to put their feet. Then the mechanism reset with a small dry click and the throat of the bell was just a hole in some brass again.

"That's it?" Dey said. "Fourteen months and that's the message?"

"That's the message," Wren said.

Salas had come two steps closer without seeming to. "That's her," he said. "That's her voice, I told you I had it, I told all of you—" and then he stopped, because he was hearing the tail of it now, the way it ended flat with nothing under the words. No tune. No lift. A woman with no air to waste, spending what she had on the shortest sentences she could build.

"Huh," Salas said.

"You had her in your ear fourteen months," Nia said, without turning round, "and you got the wrong woman."

"I heard her sing."

"She never sang. Singing's air." Nia's voice didn't rise at all, which was somehow worse. "You gave your breath to somebody you made up."

Salas opened his mouth and shut it. Fourteen months in a pocket with a valve for company, Wren thought, and that's the first time anybody's watched him with nothing queued up.

Nia's breath was going in and out through her nose, fast and shallow. Her knuckles had gone white on the handle. That was the whole of what she did. Dey shifted toward her and Wren put a hand on his arm and he stayed where he was, which for Dey was practically a religious experience.

Then the crank stopped.

Mara had let go of it. It ran a quarter turn on its own and hung there. She was sitting with her head tipped, looking at the bell the way you look at a clock in another room when it strikes and you're not sure you counted right.

"That's the order," she said, in the same voice. The same woman, whole, unhurried. "Nia first. Then Teo. Then the lid. I never know if I've got the order right."

Nobody said anything.

"Who's Teo?" she said.

The hum went out of the governor and the flyweights fell in on themselves. The needle on the lamp cell slid off its pin, down to the floor, and stayed there. The tray on the shelf that had come up bright enough to read by went the color of wet slate. Along the wall the cold-case ticked twice and quit, and on the one drawer that mattered the temperature strip came off green and started up through yellow, steady, the way a thermometer does when nothing is holding it back.

Nia still hadn't made a sound.
